identity.matching: The independent positive of the password-bytes family (287, CVE-2025-22228's 72-byte limit): the shared concern is the password's UTF-8 representation, characters against bytes. This pair adds no length restriction of its own, and encoding preservation is no authentication policy. Only the BCrypt.hashpw(String,String) entry is selected: the three-file patch also changes the cached charset in crypto.codec.Utf8 and a test utility.

mutant.description: hashpw(String, String) encodes the password with US-ASCII instead of UTF-8, so every non-ASCII character becomes '?' and different non-ASCII passwords of one length hash alike. It breaks preservation at the non-ASCII probes and keeps the ASCII ones.

notes: Concrete controls only: each revision's BCrypt class, compiled from its commit's BCrypt.java by the slice's recipe (before's checked byte for byte against Spring Security 5.2.0.M4's published class), in its own JVM, on JDK 21 and 25, over replay/probes.json's 45 probes: three valid salts from upstream's BCryptTests (the 'abc' test vector's cost-6 salt, its stored hash, and the '$2$05$' salt), never a random one, with passwords empty, ASCII, BMP non-ASCII, supplementary, 71, 72 and 73 UTF-8 bytes (in ASCII and in 2-, 3- and 4-byte characters, and with a character straddling byte 72), isolated and reversed surrogates, and null; and four invalid salts from the same tests. Observed: the returned String, or the exception's class. controls/oracle.py checks each side's lines against its statement and the two sides against each other.

On the frozen password and salt domain and the pinned JDK's charset behaviour, both revisions return the same string and throw the same exceptions. No allowed-change region. The blocker stays for the exact commits' builds, which no task here claims.

Predicted from a static scan, not from an attempt: jvmcontract gaps on BCrypt.hashpw(String,String) refuses the changed operation itself on both sides, before's String.getBytes(String) and after's String.getBytes(Charset) (an array result of a JDK instance method) and after's read of StandardCharsets.UTF_8 (a JDK static field that is not a compile-time constant); the unchanged callee adds the refused Arrays.copyOf(byte[],int) and Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder.charAt with no approximation. So the strict preservation attempt is predicted to stop at the UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion, the password-bytes family's shared demand, before the cipher.
